title: Filter with conditions
goal: Build Boolean masks and combine conditions to answer precise questions.
prerequisites: Know column selection and the basic comparison operators.

cells.title: See the True and False values first
cells.explanation: Comparing a Series with a value produces a Boolean Series, often called a mask. Each True marks a row that meets the condition. df.loc[mask, columns] keeps those rows and selects the requested columns. Keeping the mask in its own variable makes the logic easier to inspect.
cells.code:
df = students()
mask = df["Score"] > 80
print(mask)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What is the type of value at each position in mask?
questions.answer: A Boolean value, True or False, for this clean non-missing Score column.

questions.prompt: Why is df["Score"] > 80 not already the filtered table?
questions.answer: It only contains the condition results. A second selection uses that mask to retrieve the matching records.

cells.task: Change the condition to Score < 70. Select Student_ID, Name, and Score into result. Print the number of matches.
cells.hint: Change > to < and use 70 as the threshold.
cells.solution:
df = students()
mask = df["Score"] < 70
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
print("Matches:", len(result))
cells.solution_note: Dana, Hassan, and Khalid match the new rule, giving three rows. The question changed from high scores to scores needing attention.

check.prompt: What does a True in a filter mask mean?
check.feedback: A True marks a row to keep when the mask is used for selection.

cells.watch: A mask should correspond to the table being filtered; a mask from another table can misalign.
cells.takeaway: I can separate the condition from the table selection it controls.

cells.title: Combine conditions with AND and OR
cells.explanation: Use & for element-by-element AND and | for element-by-element OR. Put parentheses around each comparison before combining them. AND requires both conditions; OR requires at least one. Python's and and or do not combine pandas Series masks this way.
cells.code:
df = students()
mask = (df["Campus"] == "RAK") & (df["Score"] >= 80)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What two conditions must a row satisfy?
questions.answer: Its Campus must equal RAK and its Score must be at least 80.

questions.prompt: What changes if & is replaced by |?
questions.answer: A student can pass either condition: be at RAK, have Score at least 80, or satisfy both. More rows can qualify.

cells.task: Select students who are at RAK OR have Score at least 90. Keep the same four output columns.
cells.solution:
df = students()
mask = (df["Campus"] == "RAK") | (df["Score"] >= 90)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: All six RAK students qualify, and Fatima qualifies through her score of 95. Chloe meets both conditions but appears only once, so there are seven rows.

check.prompt: Which correctly combines two pandas conditions with AND?
check.feedback: Use & for element-wise AND; parenthesize each comparison when constructing the masks.

cells.watch: Do not omit the parentheses around comparisons; operator precedence can change the expression.
cells.takeaway: I can translate both, either, and at least into correct filter logic.

cells.title: Membership, ranges, and NOT
cells.explanation: isin() tests whether a value belongs to an allowed list. between() checks a range; inclusive="both" includes its two endpoints. The ~ operator reverses a Boolean mask. Naming masks can make a longer rule easier to explain.
cells.code:
df = students()
in_program = df["Program"].isin(["AI"])
in_range = df["Score"].between(70, 90, inclusive="both")
result = df.loc[in_program & in_range, ["Name", "Program", "Score"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What does inclusive="both" tell between() to do?
questions.answer: Include values exactly equal to 70 or 90, as well as values between them.

questions.prompt: Which AI students have scores between 70 and 90 here?
Why does isin(["AI"]) use a list even for one allowed value?
questions.answer: isin expects a list-like collection of allowed values. The same expression can later include several categories.

cells.task: Select students whose Program is NOT AI and whose Score is between 70 and 85 inclusive. Print their names, programs, and scores.
cells.hint: Reverse the membership mask with ~ and combine it with the new range mask.
cells.solution:
df = students()
not_ai = ~df["Program"].isin(["AI"])
in_range = df["Score"].between(70, 85, inclusive="both")
result = df.loc[not_ai & in_range, ["Name", "Program", "Score"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Bilal, Ethan, Ivy, and Lina qualify. ~ reverses the AI membership test before the score range is applied.

check.prompt: Which operator reverses a Boolean Series?
check.feedback: Use ~ for element-wise Boolean reversal of a pandas mask.

cells.watch: Do not use Program == ["AI", "IT"] to test membership; use .isin(["AI", "IT"]).
cells.takeaway: I can express allowed categories, numerical ranges, and excluded categories.

cells.title: Read a filter written with query
cells.explanation: query() is another way to express a row filter, using a short expression in a string. Column names appear inside that expression. @limit refers to a Python variable outside it. Learn the normal Boolean-mask form first so you can check what the query means.
cells.code:
df = students()
limit = 85
result = df.query("Score >= @limit and Campus == 'Dubai'")[["Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: Why is there an @ before limit?
questions.answer: It tells query to use the Python variable limit instead of looking for a column named limit.

questions.prompt: Which Dubai students meet the threshold?
Why is and accepted here even though a previous cell used &?
questions.answer: query parses its expression string. Outside query, combining pandas Series directly requires the element-wise operators such as &.

cells.task: Use a normal Boolean mask instead of query to find Dubai students with Score at least 80. Save the same three columns in result.
cells.solution:
df = students()
limit = 80
mask = (df["Score"] >= limit) & (df["Campus"] == "Dubai")
result = df.loc[mask, ["Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Fatima, Jamal, and Lina meet the threshold of 80. A mask and a query can express the same selection rule.

check.prompt: Inside query, what does @limit refer to?
check.feedback: @ accesses a variable from the surrounding Python scope within the query expression.

cells.watch: Use fixed, trusted query expressions for these lessons; do not construct executable expressions from arbitrary user text.
cells.takeaway: I can translate a simple query into a Boolean mask and explain both.
